lead: Water can exist as ice, liquid water or vapour. A pressure–temperature phase diagram maps which phase is stable, where two phases coexist, and where all three meet. The phase rule gives a simple freedom count; the diagram gives the shape. Engineers use it for steam generation, refrigeration, freeze-drying and weather models. Only a few universities teach the full diagram, so treat this as an advanced sketch.
prereq: You need: the phase rule from Chapter 3.4.

blocks.text: Water is a one-component system: the only component is H₂O. A phase is a physically distinct part, so ice, liquid water and vapour are three phases. Plot pressure p on the y-axis and temperature T on the x-axis. Ice is stable at low T and high p; liquid water at higher T and high p; vapour at low p or high T. Inside a region one phase exists, and T and p can change independently over a small range.

Three curves separate the regions. The sublimation curve runs to the triple point; ice and vapour coexist. The vaporization curve runs from the triple point to the critical point; liquid and vapour coexist. The fusion curve runs from the triple point upward; ice and liquid coexist. The triple point is 273.16 K and 611 Pa, where all three phases coexist. The critical point is 647 K and 22.1 MPa. Above it liquid and vapour cannot be told apart.

At equilibrium the phase rule is F = C − P + 2. F is the number of degrees of freedom: independent intensive variables you can change without losing a phase. C is the number of components. P is the number of phases. For water C = 1.

Inside a region P = 1, so F = 1 − 1 + 2 = 2. You can change T and p a little and stay in the same region. On a boundary curve P = 2, so F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1. Choose T and the curve fixes p, or choose p and it fixes T. At the triple point P = 3, so F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0. Pressure and temperature are fixed at 273.16 K and 611 Pa until one phase disappears. The same count explains why a boiling point needs a stated pressure: at 1 atm water boils at 373 K.

sections.h3: Why the fusion curve leans left

blocks.text: The fusion curve of water leans left, not right. Its slope is negative: raising pressure lowers the melting point. The Clapeyron equation gives the slope: dp/dT = ΔH_fus/(T ΔV_fus). ΔH_fus is the enthalpy of fusion, T is absolute temperature, and ΔV_fus is the volume change when ice melts. For ice to water, volume decreases, so ΔV_fus is negative. The enthalpy change is positive, so dp/dT is negative.

Most substances expand on melting, so their fusion curve leans right. Ice is unusual because its open hydrogen-bonded structure collapses on melting. A pressure increase therefore favours the denser liquid phase. The effect is small: ice melts slightly below 273.15 K under moderate pressure. This negative slope is a favourite exam point. Do not call 273.15 K and 1 atm the triple point; that is the normal melting point. The triple point is 273.16 K and 611 Pa.

figure.caption: The three curves meet at the triple point (273.16 K, 0.611 kPa); the vapour curve ends at the critical point (647 K, 22.1 MPa). Notice the fusion curve is almost vertical and leans left.

spec.aria: Schematic pressure–temperature phase diagram for water; the sublimation, vaporization and fusion curves meet at the triple point near 273.16 K and 0.611 kPa, and the vaporization curve ends at the critical point near 647 K and 22.1 MPa.

examples.question: Water has a triple point at 273.16 K and 611 Pa. Find F at the triple point and along the liquid-vapour curve.
steps: Identify the component: C = 1, because only H₂O is present.
At the triple point, P = 3: ice, liquid and vapour coexist.
Along the liquid-vapour curve, P = 2: liquid and vapour coexist.
examples.answer: F = 0 at the triple point and F = 1 along the liquid-vapour curve.
examples.check:
C = 1
F_triple = C - 3 + 2
F_curve = C - 2 + 2
print(F_triple)
print(F_curve)

traps: Calling 273.15 K and 1 atm the triple point. That is the normal melting point; the triple point is 273.16 K and 611 Pa.
Using pressure p as P in F = C − P + 2. P is the number of phases.
Saying the fusion curve has a positive slope. For water it is negative because ice is less dense than liquid water.
Forgetting that above the critical point liquid and vapour are one phase, not two.
Mixing up sublimation and vaporization: sublimation is solid to vapour, below the triple point.

quiz.q: State the phase rule and define F, C and P.
quiz.a: F = C − P + 2; F is degrees of freedom, C components, P phases.

quiz.q: Give the temperature and pressure of water's triple point.
Why is F zero at the triple point?
quiz.a: C = 1 and P = 3, so F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0; no intensive variable can change without losing a phase.

quiz.q: Why does the fusion curve of water lean left?
quiz.a: ΔV_fus is negative when ice melts, so dp/dT is negative; pressure lowers the melting point.

quiz.q: For water at 1 atm and 373 K, liquid and vapour coexist. Find F.
Explain why 273.15 K at 1 atm is not the triple point.
quiz.a: At 273.15 K and 1 atm, P = 2: ice and liquid coexist at the normal melting point. The triple point has P = 3 at 273.16 K and 611 Pa.

beyond: Not for the exam. Steam power plants use the water phase diagram to choose boiler and condenser pressures. Refrigeration cycles exploit the liquid-vapour boundary. Freeze-drying places food under vacuum below the triple point so ice sublimes instead of melting. Climate models track the same boundaries in the atmosphere. Search for 'steam tables' and 'water triple point cell' to go further.
